main.title: Galaga
main.summary: Galaga is a 1981 fixed shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: A captured ship becomes a dual fighter
cards.text: Galaga is a 1981 fixed shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released by Midway Manufacturing in North America. It is the sequel to 1979's Galaxian, and the second game in the Galaxian series. Controlling a starship, the player is tasked with destroying the Galaga forces in each stage while avoiding enemies and projectiles. "Boss Galaga" enemies can capture a player's ship via a tractor beam, which can be rescued by another ship to give the player a "dual fighter" with additional firepower.

cards.heading: Yokoyama's team changes arcade hardware
cards.text: Shigeru Yokoyama led development with a small team. Initial planning took about two months to finish. Originally developed for the Namco Galaxian arcade board, it was instead shifted to a new system as suggested by Namco's Research and Development division. Inspiration for the dual fighter mechanic was taken from a film that Yokoyama had seen prior to development, in which a ship was captured using a large circular beam. The project became immensely popular around the company, with Namco's president Masaya Nakamura even taking interest.

cards.heading: From poor location tests to a lasting arcade hit
cards.text: Although early location tests were unsuccessful, Galaga went on to become one of the most successful titles of the golden age of arcade video games, routinely appearing on Japanese and American arcade charts through 1987. It was acclaimed by critics for its engaging gameplay and for its improvements made over its predecessor, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest video games of all time. Several home ports were released for a multitude of platforms, including the MSX, Atari 7800, and NES, alongside releases on digital distribution platforms such as Xbox Live Arcade and appearances in many Namco compilations. It was followed by Gaplus in 1984.

main.title: Warlords
main.summary: Warlords is a 1981 action video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades; in Japan, it was distributed by Sega.

cards.text: Warlords is a 1981 action video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades; in Japan, it was distributed by Sega. The gameplay resembles a combination of Atari's earlier games Quadrapong (1974) and Breakout (1976), and has the player (or up to four players) attempt to destroy other castles in different corners of the screen by deflecting one or more fireballs with a shield. As with Pong and Breakout, players use paddle controllers to manipulate their shield.

Unlike most Atari arcade games of the time, Warlords began development as an Atari 2600 game that was later converted to an arcade game; the 2600 version was released shortly after the arcade version. The arcade version of Warlords came in both a two-player upright version and a four-player cocktail version. The game was considered a success, although a redesign for a smaller cabinet was necessary, as the large cabinet made it impossible to produce in large quantities and difficult to install.

main.title: Donkey Kong
main.subtitle: Donkey Kong Turns a Jump into a Grammar for Video Games
main.summary: On July 9, 1981 Nintendo began the limited Japanese arcade release of Donkey Kong.

cards.heading: Donkey Kong Turns a Jump into a Grammar for Video Games
cards.text: Donkey Kong is Nintendo's 1981 arcade platform-action game, designed by Shigeru Miyamoto. Its limited Japanese release began on 9 July. Jumpman, later known as Mario, climbs through four screens to rescue Lady from the gorilla. Ramps, barrels, conveyors and elevators change the movement required in each stage. The characters' animation connects these obstacles to a small rescue story.

cards.heading: Turning Radar Scope hardware into Donkey Kong
cards.text: The circuit board of Radar Scope was restructured for Donkey Kong. The Radar Scope hardware, originally inspired by the Namco Galaxian hardware, was designed for a large number of enemies moving around at high speeds, which Donkey Kong does not require, so the development team removed unnecessary functions and reduced the scale of the circuit board. The gameplay and graphics were reworked for updated ROM chips; the existing CPU, sound hardware, and monitor were left intact. The character set, scoreboard, upper HUD display, and font are almost identical to Radar Scope, with palette differences. The Donkey Kong hardware has the memory capacity for displaying 128 foreground sprites at 16x16 pixels each and 256 background tiles at 8x8 pixels each. Mario and all moving objects use single sprites, the taller Pauline uses two sprites, and the larger Donkey Kong uses six sprites.

cards.heading: Four screens, from rolling barrels to the final rivets
cards.text: Each of the four single-screen stages represents 25 meters of the structure Donkey Kong has climbed: 25, 50, 75, and 100 meters. Stage one involves Mario scaling a construction site made of crooked girders and ladders while jumping over or hammering barrels and oil drums tossed by Donkey Kong. Stage two involves climbing a five-story structure of conveyor belts, each of which transport cement pans. The third stage involves the player riding elevators while avoiding bouncing springs. The final stage requires Mario to remove eight rivets from the platforms supporting Donkey Kong; this causes Donkey Kong to fall and the hero to be reunited with Pauline. These four stages combine to form one level.

cards.heading: Characters made legible through animation and a few pixels
cards.text: The game uses graphics and animation for characterization. Donkey Kong smirks upon Mario's demise. Pauline has a pink dress and long hair, and a speech balloon crying "HELP!". Mario, depicted in red overalls and a red cap, is an everyman character, a type common in Japan. Graphical limitations and the low pixel resolution of the small sprites prompted his design. A mustache implies a mouth, a cap obviates the animation of hair, and colored overalls distinguish his arm movements. The artwork of the cabinets and promotional materials make these cartoon-like character designs even more explicit. Pauline, for example, is disheveled like King Kong's Fay Wray in a torn dress and stiletto heels.

main.title: Frogger
main.subtitle: The River That Teaches You to Read Movement
main.summary: Konami's Frogger, published by Sega in 1981, asks players to guide frogs across traffic and a moving river.

cards.heading: Crossing the road and river
cards.text: Frogger is a 1981 action video game developed by Konami and published by Sega for arcades. It was released in North America by Sega/Gremlin. The object of the game is to direct five frogs to their homes by dodging traffic on a busy road, then crossing a river by jumping on floating logs, turtles, and alligators.

cards.heading: Water Is a Rule, Not a Background
cards.text: Each crossing has two distinct halves. On the road, the frog must avoid vehicles travelling through horizontal lanes. At the river, touching water costs a life, so moving logs and turtles become places to land. Alligators and snakes introduce further hazards. The change asks the player to reconsider the same movement: first avoid what travels across the screen, then use moving objects to reach the other side.

cards.heading: Every Hop Is a Prediction
cards.text: The frog does not slide freely. It advances in discrete hops across a grid while cars, logs and animals continue moving sideways. A correct decision therefore depends not only on where an object is, but on where it will be when the hop ends. The timer prevents players from waiting indefinitely for a perfect pattern and turns observation into rhythm. With very few elements, Frogger asks players to read relative speeds, empty spaces and opposing directions. Difficulty grows by increasing density and variation rather than introducing a new vocabulary at every stage. It is spatial prediction compressed into seconds. The river in the second half makes this logic even clearer because the safe point keeps moving after the frog has landed on it.

cards.heading: A Simple Frog Crosses Four Decades
cards.text: Konami developed Frogger in 1981, with Sega and Gremlin bringing it to Western arcades. Its traffic and river patterns reward precision, observation and knowing when to take a risk. Ports, sequels and references carried its premise into later decades. The Strong included Frogger among its 2026 World Video Game Hall of Fame finalists, highlighting its broad appeal.

main.title: Bosconian
main.summary: Bosconian is a 1981 multidirectional shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: Shooting in both directions
cards.text: Bosconian is a 1981 multidirectional shooter video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released by Midway Manufacturing in North America. The goal is to earn as many points as possible by destroying enemy missiles and bases using a ship which shoots simultaneously both the front and back.

cards.heading: An influential arcade shooter
cards.text: Bosconian was commercially successful in Japan and received positive critical reception, but did not achieve the global commercial success of other shoot 'em ups from the golden age of arcade video games. It was ported to home computers as Bosconian '87 (1987) and spawned two sequels: Blast Off (1989) and Final Blaster (1990). Since its release, Bosconian has been regarded by critics as influential in the shoot 'em up genre.

main.title: Carol Shaw and River Raid
main.subtitle: A long flight inside four kilobytes
main.summary: Carol Shaw needed more river than a cartridge could hold. She made the landscape from rules, then tuned those rules into a game.

cards.heading: A river too long for the cartridge
cards.text: Carol Shaw developed River Raid for Activision's Atari 2600 in 1982. The player pilots an aircraft along a river, steering through narrowing banks, shooting obstacles and watching a falling fuel gauge. Fitting the long journey into a small cartridge required a way to create changing terrain without storing a separate picture of every stretch.

cards.heading: Making landscape from a sequence
cards.text: For Activision's 1982 Atari 2600 game, Shaw used a repeatable number sequence to help decide the river's changing width. Short pieces of landscape could become a much longer course. Starting from the same value reproduced the same route, giving players a world they could learn rather than an arbitrary new river on every attempt.

cards.heading: Turning a method into a challenge
cards.text: The technical solution still needed a designer. Shaw adjusted how narrow the river could become and how often fuel appeared. Steering, shooting and refuelling pulled attention in different directions. A fuel depot could be an opportunity to survive longer, while a narrow channel punished an overcorrection. The landscape's apparent size mattered because it supported those decisions.

cards.heading: The evidence behind the finished game
cards.text: Shaw's surviving papers include code, working notes and design material. They preserve stages of building the game alongside the finished cartridge. The records help explain the terrain-generation method and the adjustments through which its repeating sequence became a route players could learn.

features.title: A river made from rules
features.summary: Shaw turned a repeatable terrain sequence into a controlled challenge.

cards.heading: Generating a river
cards.text: River Raid needed a scrolling route within the Atari 2600's cartridge space. Shaw used a repeatable sequence to generate terrain and set limits on what it could produce. This allowed the program to construct a continuous-looking river from a smaller amount of stored information. The sequence supplied the landscape while her restrictions shaped the passages the player would encounter.

cards.heading: Before the finished display
cards.text: Shaw’s papers at The Strong contain notes, sketches, design documents and source-code printouts. Its historical account describes Atari-era graphics drawn on graph paper and translated into numerical values, with code also written by hand before being entered. These materials preserve intermediate forms of work that a cartridge does not show. A small on-screen shape could begin as a marked square on paper; an instruction could exist first as handwriting. Following those forms makes the programmer’s decisions more visible than treating the finished display as something the computer produced alone.

cards.heading: Designing the challenge
cards.text: Generating terrain did not settle the design. Shaw described restrictions on how narrow the river could become as the game progressed, turning an economical representation into a controlled challenge. Her conversation with Al Miller also helped move the idea away from another space setting. The aircraft, river and fuel created a different situation to read. This is where programming and design meet: the sequence supplies material, but the designer decides what kinds of passages it may produce and what the player must manage along the route.

cards.heading: Preserving the code
cards.text: The Strong identifies River Raid source printouts among papers spanning Shaw's work at Atari and Activision. Its collection places code alongside advertisements and career records. Staff manage access to some scans because the connected sheets of paper need careful handling. The listings preserve the program's instructions in a physical form that also requires maintenance and protection.

main.title: Commodore 64
main.subtitle: A computer with a voice
main.summary: The SID sound chip helped turn a mass-market home computer into a musical instrument.

cards.heading: A computer with a distinctive voice
cards.text: Introduced in 1982, the Commodore 64 brought games, programming and music-making into the same beige case. Its SID audio chip gave composers control over distinctive waveforms and filters, producing a sound that musicians still explore.

cards.heading: Making more from familiar hardware
cards.text: The machine's history includes commercial games, copied magazine programs and the demoscene: communities building audiovisual works to test what the hardware could do. Creative use continued long after the computer ceased being new.

features.title: Rob Hubbard: programming the performance
features.summary: Three channels can change their jobs.

cards.heading: A channel changes roles
cards.text: A bass part and a percussion part need not own separate channels throughout a piece. Explaining his Commodore 64 work in 1986, Hubbard described software switching patches between notes. A channel could serve the bass, then become percussion a little later. The arrangement was written around those handovers. What sounded like several continuing parts depended on their events fitting together without requiring more simultaneous notes than the machine supplied. Composition therefore included deciding when one apparent instrument could temporarily make room for another to be heard.

cards.heading: The code bends a note
cards.text: Hubbard's playback interpreter did more than read a list of pitches. It drove the chip through routines for changing the sound while a note continued. He described generating vibrato in software rather than sacrificing another channel as an oscillator, and switching rapidly from noise to another waveform. A sustained note could contain a sequence of programmed gestures. The performance was thus partly written in the replay code: changing a routine could change the character of an instrument without changing the melody that called for it.

cards.heading: A melody has a past
cards.text: Looking back in 2001, Hubbard explained that some melodies used in games had been written years earlier. A commission might come with directions from a programmer, or leave the musical choice to him. Film and pop music could also provide starting points. He adapted this material to the sound hardware and the particular game he was working on.

cards.heading: An arrangement leaves something out
cards.text: For an orchestral version of WAR, Hubbard omitted the original second section because he felt it did not suit that arrangement. He described the result as one interpretation and imagined other approaches. Work with Chris Abbott on the Back In Time projects involved further collaboration and decisions about which parts of the Commodore music to retain or change.

features.title: Making something of the wait
features.summary: Artists and programmers fill loading time.

cards.heading: Interpret the picture
cards.text: Paul Docherty struggled with the complicated artwork behind his first paid loading screen, Leviathan. Rich Hare, who had helped him obtain the job, offered a useful correction: adapt the design to the Commodore instead of copying every detail. The computer's limited picture became a problem of interpretation. An artist had to decide what carried the image and what could change. Docherty later remembered that advice as a turning point, when knowing the machine became part of drawing well for it.

cards.heading: Dithering with a purpose
cards.text: Druid II gave Docherty a chance to answer an artist he admired. Bob Stevenson's earlier Druid picture set a standard for economical drawing, and Docherty remembered taking particular pride in the sequel's loading screen. He described using enough dithering to blend colours, then varying the technique in later pictures. Deadlines remained tight, but each screen offered another experiment in how a few marks could suggest form. Before the game itself appeared, its illustrator was already giving the player something to look at.

cards.heading: The loader makes room
cards.text: Paul Hughes traced Freeload to his frustration with slow Commodore tapes. He changed the timing approach so that loading could continue while the main processor did other work. Keeping the screen visible grew into music, animation and scrolling during the wait. His account credits composers Martin Galway, Peter Clarke and Jonathan Dunn, alongside several loading-screen artists. The experience remembered as an Ocean loader joined their work to the code moving data from tape. A utilitarian interval became a small audiovisual production of its own.

cards.heading: A cheaper tape needs music
cards.text: Faster was not always cheaper. Hughes remembered that less expensive duplicating equipment used for Hit Squad budget releases struggled with Freeload's short pulses. He slowed the system down so the tapes could be manufactured reliably. That decision made the wait longer than the existing music, and Jonathan Dunn had to supply a piece lasting another minute. Price, factory equipment and composition met inside one loading sequence. The player heard the consequence of a manufacturing compromise before reaching the game they had bought.

features.title: Learning the chip by ear
features.summary: SID joins a designer's choices with a reader's experiments.

cards.heading: A synthesizer on a chip
cards.text: Bob Yannes approached the SID chip as somebody interested in electronic music. In his 1996 interview, he described wanting to put a synthesizer onto one piece of silicon. Time and chip area shaped what survived that ambition. Three complete oscillators took space that might otherwise have supported further features, and a planned pitch table was left for software to supply. The Commodore's voice grew from those choices: music hardware made within a production schedule, with some jobs handed to its programmers.

cards.heading: Choosing the shape of a note
cards.text: The response of a note was chosen by listening. Yannes recalled comparing the envelope behaviour with a Sequential Circuits Pro-1 synthesizer, then selecting a limited set of useful rates. The chip could not offer every possible adjustment, so its designer had to decide which changes musicians would receive. This was an act of instrument making inside the electronics. A register value was also a choice about how a sound begins, holds and fades, turning a restricted control range into a particular set of expressive possibilities.

cards.heading: Type a melody
cards.text: Commodore's Programmer's Reference Guide invited readers to begin without being expert musicians or programmers. Its first sound example supplied a short BASIC program and explained the lines individually. The melody became groups of numbers describing pitch and duration; the program read each group, started a note, waited and released it. A reader could type the sequence, save it and hear the result. The printed page connected the chip to a repeatable exercise, making an electronic instrument accessible through ordinary commands and a little patient transcription.

cards.heading: Change two numbers and listen
cards.text: The guide then returned to that same melody to change its tone. Replacing two control values switched the sawtooth waveform to a triangle, leaving the note data in place. Readers were asked to run the program again and hear the difference. The exercise separated what was played from the character of the instrument playing it. Instead of requiring a new song for every experiment, the manual gave the learner something stable to compare, then made a small edit audible as a change in sound.

main.title: Bump 'n' Jump
main.summary: Bump 'n' Jump, also known in Japan as Burnin' Rubber, is a 1982 vehicular combat video game developed and published by Data East for arcades.

cards.text: Bump 'n' Jump, also known in Japan as Burnin' Rubber, is a 1982 vehicular combat video game developed and published by Data East for arcades. Released in North America by Bally Midway, the arcade version was available as both a dedicated board and as part of Data East's DECO Cassette System. The goal is to drive to the end of a course while knocking enemy vehicles into the sides of the track and jumping over large obstacles like bodies of water.

The arcade game was a commercial success in Japan and North America. It was ported to the Atari 2600, Intellivision, ColecoVision, Nintendo Entertainment System, and Sharp X1. The Famicom version of Burnin' Rubber was published as Buggy Popper in Japan in October 1986.

main.title: Pitfall!
main.summary: Pitfall! is a 1982 platform video game developed by David Crane and published by Activision for the Atari 2600.

cards.text: Pitfall! is a 1982 platform video game developed by David Crane and published by Activision for the Atari 2600. The player controls Pitfall Harry, who has a time limit of 20 minutes to seek treasure in a jungle. The game world is populated by enemies and hazards that variously cause the player to lose lives or points. Pitfall! was ported to the Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit computers, ColecoVision, Commodore 64, and MSX.

Crane had made several games for both Atari, Inc. and Activision before working on Pitfall! in 1982. He started with creating a realistic-style walking animation for a person on the Atari 2600 hardware, then fashioned a game around it. He used a jungle setting with items to collect and enemies to avoid, and the result became Pitfall!

Pitfall! received positive reviews at the time of its release praising both its gameplay and graphics. It was influential in the platform game genre, and various publications have considered it as being amongst the greatest video games of all time. It is also one of the best-selling Atari 2600 video games, as well as the best-selling Atari 2600 game that’s not an arcade port. It has been included in various Activision compilation games and was included as a secret extra in later Activision-published titles. A more advanced sequel, Pitfall II: Lost Caverns, was released in 1984.

features.title: A name inside the box
features.summary: Authorship helps players choose a game.

cards.heading: Choosing an author
cards.text: David Crane recalled crediting designers as one reason for forming Activision. President Jim Levy brought record-industry experience to promoting the people behind its games. Crane compared this with book publishing: players who enjoyed one designer's work could look for another game by that person. A name on the product became part of how Activision presented its catalogue.

cards.heading: The colleagues in the room
cards.text: Activision's designers had their own projects, but played one another's work and discussed changes. Crane recalled giving Pitfall! a single life shortly before release, until colleagues persuaded him to allow more attempts. Their testing and arguments affected the final rules, even while individual designers received a prominent credit.

cards.heading: Advice from the maker
cards.text: The Pitfall! booklet names Crane as designer, lists his earlier games and includes his advice. He suggests considering travel to the left, learning underground routes and planning a journey. Players could connect these practical tips with the named person who had constructed the challenge.

cards.heading: A score leaves the television
cards.text: The booklet offered entry to Pitfall Harry's Explorers' Club for players reaching 20,000 points. They had to photograph the television score and send the picture by post. Crane's advice also invited letters. The club gave a player a reason to share an achievement beyond the living room, with the photograph and correspondence connecting that performance to Activision.

main.title: Pengo
main.summary: Pengo is a 1982 maze video game developed by Coreland and published by Sega for arcades.

cards.text: Pengo is a 1982 maze video game developed by Coreland and published by Sega for arcades. The player controls Pengo, a red penguin who resides in the Antarctic. The game takes place in an overhead maze made of ice blocks, where Pengo crushes blob-like Sno-Bees by sliding blocks into them. The objective is to survive each round by eliminating all Sno-Bees and Sno-Bee eggs, while optionally lining up the three diamond blocks to earn a large score bonus.

There are two versions of the arcade game: the first uses "Popcorn" as the theme, and the second has original music. There are other small differences as well. Pengo was ported to the Atari 2600, Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit computers, and Game Gear.
